🚀 Team ASTROFIX – Junior Astronaut Training Mission

We are ASTROFIX, a passionate and innovative team participating in the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. Our challenge, Junior Astronaut Training Mission, aims to make space exploration exciting, interactive, and educational for young aspiring astronauts.
summary:
MARS MAYHEM – An Interactive Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer

MARS MAYHEM is an interactive, offline, browser-based 3D Mars-colony simulator developed for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. Players take command of a four-member astronaut crew and manage a Martian outpost, balancing essential resources such as power, water, oxygen and food while assigning crew members to scientific research, agriculture, engineering and life-support operations.

Through an explorable colony, interactive facilities and ROVER-01, players collect resources, research new technologies and operate a fuel-production system to manufacture the propellant needed for the return journey to Earth. Dust storms, marsquakes, radiation warnings and equipment failures challenge players to make informed decisions as the mission progresses.

MARS MAYHEM addresses the challenge by transforming astronaut responsibilities into an interactive, decision-driven learning experience. It makes the complexities of sustaining human life beyond Earth tangible, encouraging young learners to develop critical thinking, resource management, teamwork and problem-solving skills — essential capabilities for future space exploration.
details:
MARS MAYHEM: AN INTERACTIVE MARS OUTPOST SURVIVAL AND MISSION TRAINER

Developed for: NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026
Challenge: Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer
Team: ASTRO FIX

1. Project Overview — What Did We Develop?

MARS MAYHEM is an interactive, browser-based 3D Mars-colony survival and astronaut mission-training simulator. Developed in response to NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, it places the player in the role of a commander responsible for managing a four-member astronaut crew stranded on Mars after one of three return rockets is unable to depart because of insufficient p5.ropellant.

The mission is not simply to survive for ten Martian days (sols). Players must keep all four astronauts alive, maintain the colony's life-support systems, conduct scientific research, collect essential resources, manufacture rocket propellant, fuel the return vehicle, and successfully bring the crew back to Earth.

The game follows the principle: SURVIVE MARS. BUILD YOUR FUEL. FIND YOUR WAY HOME.

It is designed as an educational experience in which students learn by making decisions, managing interconnected systems, responding to emergencies, and observing the consequences of their actions.

2. How Does the Project Work?

Players explore a fully modelled 3D Martian outpost from a third-person astronaut perspective. They can walk around the colony, interact with facility consoles, manage crew assignments, operate machines, monitor resources, and control the progress of the mission.

The colony contains interconnected facilities, including solar power arrays, water processing, oxygen production, a greenhouse, a science laboratory, crew accommodation, a shelter bunker, a rover bay, a fuel-processing plant, and a launch site.

The four-member crew consists of the commander, a scientist, a botanist, and an engineer. Each specialist contributes to the colony through different assignments. Astronauts also require rest, and fatigue affects their productivity and the efficiency of the mission.

The player must balance five important areas:

  • Power: Solar arrays generate electricity for the colony. Dust accumulation and storms reduce their output, making maintenance and energy conservation essential.
  • Water: Water is obtained through rover-collected Martian ice and processed at AQUA-Core. It is shared between crew consumption, crops, and fuel production.
  • Oxygen: The O₂-MOXIE facility produces breathable oxygen when it has sufficient power and is functioning correctly.
  • Food: The BIO-Dome grows crops that require water, lighting, and time. Assigning the botanist helps automate agricultural operations.
  • Crew welfare: Astronauts must rest regularly. Fatigue reduces productivity and can eventually threaten crew survival.

The systems are interconnected. For example, a power shortage can interrupt oxygen production, while using too much water for fuel manufacturing can leave insufficient water for the crew and crops.

3. ROVER-01 and Resource Collection

ROVER-01 is a physically modelled, controllable-by-mission autonomous rover that travels across the Martian terrain to investigate and collect resources.

Players can select four types of missions:

  • Water-Ice Survey
  • Carbon Collection
  • Oxygen Resource Survey
  • Hydrogen Collection

The rover follows a visible route, travels to a resource deposit, performs its collection operation, and returns to the colony. Some fuel-material missions have a 40% prospecting chance, meaning a mission may return without finding usable material.

The resource deposits are finite, so players must plan their missions carefully rather than repeatedly collecting unlimited supplies. The rover also consumes power, can experience breakdowns, and requires maintenance.

4. Scientific Research and Return-Fuel Production

Research is an essential part of the mission. The SCI-Lab contains seven research topics, including Martian Soil Analysis, Solar Power Efficiency, Water-Ice Extraction, Crop Growth in Martian Conditions, Oxygen Production from CO₂, Radiation Shielding Materials, and Martian Fuel Production Technology.

Three research topics must be completed, and Martian Fuel Production Technology is compulsory.

After unlocking the required technology, players can operate the FUEL-PROCESSOR to manufacture the propellant needed for the return journey. The process requires three separate feedstocks: carbon, oxygen, and hydrogen. These materials must be collected or produced in sufficient quantities, and the plant also requires electricity.

The manufactured propellant is transferred to the M3 return rocket at the LAUNCH-SITE. The launch system checks ten journey-home objectives before allowing the rocket to depart. Therefore, surviving ten sols alone does not mean the mission has been completed.

5. Environmental Challenges and Emergency Events

The colony is exposed to changing environmental and operational conditions. A random-event system introduces hazards that require players to respond quickly and manage resources carefully.

These include:

  • Dust devils and dust storms that reduce visibility and solar-power generation.
  • Marsquakes that shake the environment and may damage equipment.
  • Solar radiation events that require the crew to take shelter.
  • Greenhouse faults that interrupt agricultural operations.
  • Seal malfunctions that cause oxygen leaks at facilities.
  • Rover breakdowns that interrupt resource collection.
  • Meteorite impacts that can damage colony equipment.
  • Random failures affecting important systems such as solar arrays, water processing, and oxygen production.

Players receive warnings and must decide whether to repair equipment themselves, assign the engineer, conserve resources, or shelter the crew.

6. NASA DONKI Space Weather Monitoring System

An additional feature of MARS MAYHEM is its NASA SPACE WEATHER MONITOR, which connects the game to the Community Coordinated Modeling Center's Database of Notifications, Knowledge, and Information (DONKI).

When an internet connection is available, the monitor retrieves recent space-weather information from NASA's official CCMC DONKI API. It checks four event categories:

  • Solar Flares (FLR): Solar activity events, with available flare classifications.
  • Coronal Mass Ejections (CME): Solar eruptions and associated analysis information.
  • Solar Energetic Particles (SEP): Particle events that are particularly relevant to space-weather radiation awareness.
  • Geomagnetic Storms (GST): Geomagnetic activity information, primarily describing conditions near Earth.

The monitor displays event categories, available classifications, event times, connection status, recent records, and a game-side risk advisory. It uses a colour-coded system with green, yellow, orange, and red levels to communicate the interpreted level of concern.

For relevant solar energetic particle events, the game highlights the SHELTER-BUNKER and reminds players to review crew radiation-protection procedures. The system also connects its advisory to the existing Radiation Shielding Materials research.

An important scientific distinction is maintained: DONKI does not directly measure radiation exposure at the Martian colony or forecast Martian dust storms. Its colour levels and recommended actions are game-side interpretations, not official NASA severity ratings. Dust storms, Marsquakes, and equipment failures continue to come from the game's own simulation system.

The DONKI integration is optional. It refreshes periodically, caches previously retrieved information, and handles network errors and unavailable data. When the internet is unavailable, the game continues normally and displays:

NASA LIVE DATA UNAVAILABLE — SIMULATION MODE ACTIVE.

This allows the project to combine real NASA space-weather information with an independent, fully playable Mars-colony simulation.

7. What Benefits Does the Project Have?

MARS MAYHEM turns complex space-exploration concepts into an interactive learning experience. Instead of simply reading about the challenges of establishing a human settlement on Mars, students actively experience the responsibilities involved in managing one.

Its educational benefits include:

  • Scientific understanding: Introduces concepts such as Martian resources, solar energy, atmospheric processing, water recycling, controlled-environment agriculture, and radiation protection.
  • Critical thinking: Encourages players to evaluate situations and choose appropriate responses to changing mission conditions.
  • Resource management: Demonstrates why power, water, oxygen, food, and fuel must be carefully balanced.
  • Problem-solving: Challenges players to identify faults, respond to emergencies, and restore important colony systems.
  • Teamwork and responsibility: Demonstrates how different specialists contribute to a shared mission and why crew welfare matters.
  • Technology awareness: Introduces students to robotics, simulation, 3D environments, scientific research, and real space-weather information.

The project provides a safe virtual environment in which young learners can explore the complexity of human space exploration through experimentation and decision-making.

8. Intended Impact

Our aim is to make space science more engaging, understandable, and accessible to students.

MARS MAYHEM encourages young learners to think beyond the idea of simply travelling to another planet. It demonstrates that a successful Mars mission requires sustainable life-support systems, reliable energy, scientific research, resource extraction, engineering, crew management, and careful planning for the return journey.

By combining an interactive simulation with real NASA DONKI space-weather information, the project also introduces students to how scientific observations can support awareness and decision-making in space missions.

We hope the project inspires students to explore careers and further learning in space science, astronomy, robotics, software development, engineering, and planetary research.

9. Tools, Programming Languages, and Technologies Used

MARS MAYHEM is a software-only project developed using web technologies.

Development technologies:

  • Three.js r128: Used to create and render the interactive 3D Martian environment, astronaut, colony facilities, rover, and cinematic sequences.
  • JavaScript (ES Modules): Powers the simulation, player movement, crew management, resource systems, research, random events, rover operations, fuel production, and game logic.
  • HTML5: Structures the game interface, title screen, HUD, consoles, and information panels.
  • CSS3: Creates the visual design, mission-control interface, resource meters, warning banners, and responsive interface elements.
  • Python: Used for a lightweight local HTTP hosting script based on Python's standard library.
  • PowerShell: Provides an alternative lightweight hosting script for Windows.
  • NASA CCMC DONKI API: Supplies optional live space-weather records.
  • Web Audio API: Supports procedural sound effects and audio feedback.
  • LocalStorage: Stores saved mission progress and cached DONKI information in the browser.

The project uses locally bundled Three.js and does not require a build system, external asset downloads, or a permanent internet connection for normal gameplay.

Hardware: No physical hardware is required. MARS MAYHEM is a software-based simulation designed for desktop browsers with WebGL support.

10. What Makes the Project Creative and Innovative?

The creativity of MARS MAYHEM comes from combining several connected systems into one continuous mission rather than presenting separate educational activities.

First, the player physically explores a 3D Martian colony as an astronaut instead of controlling only a menu or a rover. Facilities are interactive, crew members move to their assigned workstations, and the rover visibly travels across the terrain.

Second, the game connects life-support management to the final objective of returning to Earth. Water is shared between the crew, crops, and hydrogen production. Electricity supports almost every facility. Research unlocks technologies, and resource collection determines whether the return rocket can be fuelled.

Third, the mission includes a complete narrative journey, with an opening cinematic showing the rocket departure and the crew left behind, followed by an ending cinematic showing the successful return to Earth. The mission report evaluates the player's performance.

Finally, the NASA DONKI integration adds a real-world scientific information layer to the simulation. Players can see actual reported space-weather events alongside clearly labelled simulated Martian hazards.

The result is an experience that combines storytelling, exploration, simulation, resource strategy, science education, and real data awareness.

11. Factors Considered During Development

While developing the project, our team considered several important factors:

  1. Scientific relevance: We used real space-exploration concepts, including solar power, resource extraction, water recycling, oxygen production, agriculture, fuel manufacturing, and radiation protection.
  2. Educational suitability: The gameplay was designed to make complex ideas understandable and engaging for young learners.
  3. System interdependence: Resources and facilities were connected so that decisions in one area could affect the entire colony.
  4. Mission realism: Crew fatigue, limited resources, equipment failures, environmental hazards, and the need for a return journey were included to demonstrate the challenges of sustaining human life beyond Earth.
  5. Accessibility: The game runs in a desktop browser and does not require specialised hardware, installation of a game engine, or an internet connection for normal gameplay.
  6. Scientific integrity: Gameplay values are simplified for educational balance and are not presented as real engineering specifications. NASA DONKI information is distinguished from game-generated hazards and from the game's own risk interpretations.
  7. Reliability: Offline functionality, saved progress, independent simulation systems, and error handling were considered so that network problems do not interrupt the mission.
  8. User experience: The team considered clear controls, readable telemetry, warning messages, interactive consoles, visual feedback, and a structured difficulty system.

12. Final Vision

MARS MAYHEM is our attempt to transform the challenges of human exploration of Mars into an experience that students can explore, understand, and learn from.

It demonstrates that reaching Mars is only one part of the challenge. Sustaining life, managing limited resources, responding to unexpected events, developing new technologies, and preparing a safe journey home are equally important.

Four astronauts. One colony. Countless challenges. One journey home.

Our goal is to inspire the next generation of explorers, scientists, and engineers by giving them the opportunity to experience the responsibilities of a Martian mission commander.

SWIM Map Shows Subsurface Water Ice on Mars:Credit	NASA/JPL-Caltech/Planetary Science Institute:The blue areas on this map of Mars show regions where NASA missions have detected subsurface water ice. Scientists can use the map – part of the Subsurface Water Ice Mapping project, or SWIM – to decide where the first astronauts to set foot on the Red Planet should land. Triangles on the map are past and present Mars missions; circles are ice-exposing impact craters.  Mars has both water ice and carbon dioxide ice (dry ice); water ice would be a critical resource for the first astronauts to step foot on Mars, who can use it for drinking, rocket fuel, and other purposes. The more water ice these astronauts land next to, the less they need to bring with them.  Because the Martian atmosphere is so thin – less than 1% the pressure experienced at sea level on Earth – liquid water is unstable on the Red Planet and will vaporize unless it’s frozen. But water ice on the planet’s surface is only stable at high latitudes that are far too cold for astronauts and robots to survive. So SWIM attempts to locate water ice preserved within the subsurface in the mid-latitudes, where landing would be feasible. Such regions are far enough toward the pole for water ice to be plentiful, but close enough to the equator to avoid the coldest temperatures seen on Mars.  SWIM combines data from several NASA missions, including the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter (MRO), 2001 Mars Odyssey, and the now-inactive Mars Global Surveyor. The project mapped the area from the equator to 60 degrees north latitude.  SWIM is led by the Planetary Science Institute in Tucson, Arizona, and managed by NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California. The University of Arizona, in Tucson, operates HiRISE, which was built by Ball Aerospace & Technologies Corp., in Boulder, Colorado. JPL, a division of Caltech in Pasadena, California, manages MRO for NASA’s Science Mission Directorate in Washington.
projectRefs: Growing healthy food in space and in remote areas.Living a healthy, sustainable lifestyle can be a challenge for all of us, but it can be especially difficult in remote areas on Earth—and also in space. As part of plans to send astronauts farther into the solar system, the Canadian Space Agency (CSA) is working with its partners to learn how to grow healthy food in harsh environments, both in space and on Earth.  In July 2026, The Growcer Inc. was awarded a contract totalling $745,000 and will work with Arctic Fresh Group of Companies, an Inuit-owned enterprise in Nunavut, to co-develop a concept for a deployable Controlled Environment Agriculture (CEA) unit.  Background Astronauts living aboard the International Space Station (ISS) receive shipments of fresh food every few months. These deliveries supplement their menu, adding variety and nutrition—important factors in keeping crewmembers healthy and happy. But as missions venture to more distant destinations like the Moon or Mars, astronauts will need to be more self-sufficient. Greater distances will make resupply trips less frequent or impossible. Instead, space travellers will need to develop "green thumbs" to grow their own food in space.
